utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning. Today we are to hear evidence of KDZ 041 via videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there are some matters to deal with before we start hearing the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, there are two matters. First of all, I understand the witness has with him some notes in -- where he is now and he wishes to refer to them during his evidence, and I've -- he may wish to address the Chamber on that. I've advised him that it would be better if he put those notes to one side during his evidence and simply testified without referring to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us deal with it by ear. Yes, thank you for the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The other matter is the motion which we filed confidentially, perhaps we could go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, before we bring in the witness, Mr. President, if I could be heard on a motion concerning the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We would like to make a motion to postpone the cross-examination of this witness. It was revealed to us first in the motion that we received late last night that I don't think Mr. Karadzic has received yet himself, but it was revealed that the witness had given testimony in a state court proceeding in Bosnia about these same events, and then more details were provided to us this morning by the Prosecution that the testimony took place in 2009. Now, this is a witness who we have only prior statements from, no prior -- this witness hasn't testified in any previous proceedings, and therefore, the testimony of this -- the transcript of this testimony would be the only opportunity we would have to review any cross-examination material or questions by a judge. So we think that it's more significant than it might otherwise be in an ordinary case. The witness declined to be interviewed by our Defence team so we didn't have the opportunity to even find out about the fact that the witness had given prior testimony. As we've said, it wasn't disclosed to us until last evening. Now, you know that we have filed a motion for the Prosecution to be ordered to inquire of its witnesses and obtain for us prior statements of witnesses or testimony in other trials in state proceedings which are not in their possession, and we recognise that you denied that motion on the 12th of January of 2011. And also, on the 8th of February, we take into account the fact that you told Dr. Karadzic not to tilt at windmills, as it were, and pursue every possible document from other proceedings and you told him to consult with experienced Defence counsel about that. And I'm an experienced Defence counsel and I'll tell you that my own experience is that these prior statements and particularly prior testimony are of a lot of importance in assessing the credibility of witnesses. If you look at the judgement in the Rwamakuba case at the ICTR, you'll see that that case was an incidence where witnesses testified under pseudonyms for the Prosecution in Arusha and then went back to Rwanda and made many testimonies in Gacaca proceedings, in front of their own people and under their own names, and those testimonies were very different than the testimonies they had given with pseudonyms in Arusha. And as a result of that, Mr. Rwamakuba was acquitted because those testimonies undermined the testimony in court. And since then, in many cases at the ICTR, Gacaca proceeding testimonies and, indeed, state court proceeding testimonies have been found to undermine the credibility of Prosecution witnesses. So we feel that there is at least a good reason why we should have access to the cross-examination and the testimony of this witness before conducting our cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If I can respond, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, we don't have a copy of the transcript in question. Second, we discovered yesterday at about 3.15 p.m. that the witness had previously testified before the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Third, he testified as a protected witness in those proceedings. Now, obviously where a person testifies as a protected witness in domestic proceedings, there is a concern that we do not violate any protective measures in force in those domestic proceedings. Fourth, the witness did consent today to the disclosure of this fact of his prior testimony to the Karadzic Defence, and within minutes of his consent, we informed the Karadzic Defence of that. Finally, as for the correct remedy, in my submission, the correct remedy is for cross-examination to continue today, for the Defence to get a copy of the transcript in question, they can then review the transcript in question and then can do one of two things. They can either tender that transcript for admission before the Court, without recalling the witness, or they can make an application to recall the witness for further cross-examination. But I think we should go ahead today with at least an initial cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it is a violation or not is one thing, but one thing -- and the -- to have a proper preparation is quite another. Yes Mr. Tieger? Do you have any observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to make one, Your Honour, but it's on the heels of a conversation I had with Mr. Robinson this morning. And following that conversation, I was surprised that the -- that it was up to Mr. Gaynor to clarify that what Mr. Robinson knew, that is that we had just received that, that we are -- that we have been engaged in precisely -- in fulfilling precisely the agreement reached with the accused to inquire of witnesses during the course of making travel arrangements and during their proofing about such matters. It didn't arise here because this witness was in Sarajevo. Mr. Robinson sent an e-mail earlier today about this. We had a discussion about it. He agreed that the Prosecution is acting in full good faith and in a proactive manner and in accordance with the agreement to obtain information about prior testimonies. So I apologise for raising that. I wouldn't have, although I was a little concerned about the fact that there might have been an implication left in the manner in which Mr. Robinson raised this issue. I wasn't going to rise. But since the Court raised the possibility of a violation, I thought I needed to do so because there is no issue about that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant to say although it is not a violation of any disclosure obligation, we need to consider whether Defence has some time to review the transcript. That was the point. Probably I was not clear. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, for myself, I certainly didn't understand Mr. Robinson to be criticising the Prosecution. And from what I've heard, it seems to me, for myself, I would have thought the Prosecution had behaved perfectly in this case. But, Mr. Robinson, might there not be some value in cross-examining today, seeing what answers are given, and then having something concrete to compare with the transcript of the other proceedings as and when you get them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that, but I actually think when we have absolutely no prior cross-examination of this witness before to actually embark on a cross-examination with -- essentially without the benefit of that might be more detrimental than beneficial to us in this case. In other cases, where we are talking about one additional statement or -- such as with General Smith or with Captain Rechner, when this issue arose before, we didn't ask that the testimony be postponed. We just reserved the right to try to call them back if we learned anything from their other testimonies. But here, when we have absolutely no other prior testimony of a witness, I think it would be more detrimental than beneficial to launch a cross-examination and then try to patch it up later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber -- before we consider the matter, can I ask, just in case, Mr. Gaynor, whether the next witness is available?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness is in The Hague but I do not believe he's been brought from his hotel just yet. Could I point out one matter in private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We granted the image distortion on the same ground on which we granted the pseudonym to this witness. Yes, Mr. Gaynor, you just informed me that the computer is now working.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with the suggestion made by Mr. Gaynor, so we decided to go to hear the cross-examination by the Defence, but we'll favourably consider when Defence makes a motion to recall the witness on the ground of the newly disclosed transcript. Yes. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The witness is ready to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly take the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you are already aware, for security reasons you will be called as just Mr. Witness or with your pseudonym, which is KDZ041, and any other people outside the courtroom will not be able to see your image. Do you understand? Are you following what I'm saying, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me now, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we seem to have a technical problem. I'm just calling for some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you follow in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it appears that the problem persists, so kindly bear with us until we get some technical help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Somebody's on his way now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we adjourn for ten minutes? That seems to be a sensible solution. We'll adjourn for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 9.33 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness, again. Do you follow the proceedings in the language you understand? I will try again. Mr. Witness, do you follow the proceedings in the language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Probably you are already aware, in any event I want to double check, for security reasons you will be called as just Mr. Witness or by your pseudonym, which is KDZ041. Therefore -- and you will be granted the protective measures of image distortion, which means people outside this courtroom will not be able to see your image. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Furthermore, whenever we discuss matters which may reveal your identity, we will go into private session, thereby the people outside the courtroom will not be able to follow the proceedings and the transcript of which will not be revealed to the public. And one matter I wanted to clarify with you is that you want to take a break every hour? My question is how long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long should that break be? I.e., how long do you need to take a break every hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 15 and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will take a 20-minutes break every hour. Yes, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the witness has taken the oath yet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it correct that you've previously provided statements to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and you've provided information to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up 65 ter 90224.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: While that's coming, Witness, did you, with the assistance of an interpreter, review an amalgamated statement which contains relevant portions of information which you provided in previous witness statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that is your name on the first page of that document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you were questioned today about the same events, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I seek admission of that document under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2310, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to read a summary for the public of the evidence which has just been admitted. The witness speaks about events in the Novi Grad municipality. Momcilo Krajisnik was the principal SDS figure in the area. Other Serb military and political leaders in the area included Jovan Tintor, Nikola Stanisic and Ranko Torbica. Nikola Stanisic and Ranko Torbica told Muslim inhabitants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now do you follow the proceedings, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Nikola Stanisic and Ranko Torbica told the Muslim inhabitants of Ahatovici that they would be attacked if they did not vacate the village. Armed Serb groups threatened and harassed the local population. By May 1992, Serb families had vacated areas surrounding Ahatovici. Serb paramilitaries including Arkanovci and White Eagles came to the area. By mid-May, telephone and electricity were disconnected. On 27th May 1992, Serb forces with tanks and armoured vehicles took up positions around Ahatovici and ordered the Muslim inhabitants to surrender. There was limited resistance. A stronger attack was launched by the Serb forces a couple of days later. 15 to 20 Muslim inhabitants were killed and about 130 houses damaged or destroyed. The witness attempted to escape in a group of about 30 men but was caught by Serb forces. The group was split in two and about 15 men were executed by the Serb forces. Jovan Tintor was present shortly after the execution and ordered that the surviving men be taken away. The Muslim men from Ahatovici were taken to a location outside a supermarket near Butile barracks. Several men were taken away in groups of four and were viciously beaten by Serb soldiers and local Serbs. The Muslim men were taken and detained in two empty fuel cisterns located next to the army barracks at Rajlovac. While detained at the cisterns, the men were taken out and beaten severely. The commander of those guarding the cisterns was Mile Stojanovic. The witness was one of approximately 55 prisoners who were taken out of one of the cisterns, placed on a bus and driven by a man called Zuti towards Semizovac. Zuti was said to be the driver of Jovan Tintor. The bus was escorted by four vehicles which contained armed men. The bus was stopped in the village of Sokolina. The men on the bus were ordered not to get up or they would be shot. Shortly after the guards and driver had got off the bus, the bus was fired upon for about 15 minutes. Almost all the men on the bus were killed. That ends the public summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, I want to take you now to the moment during the attack on Ahatovici where your group of 30 men were arrested. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. Half of the people were killed, half were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is at the top of page 7 for the other participants in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, you said that half of the people were killed and I want you to describe what exactly you saw during that incident.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: When we tried to make a breakthrough to the nearby forest and head onwards to Visoko, fierce infantry fire was opened from the forest and from the surrounding area at a group that was in a plum grove. Some ten men were either shot dead or wounded. I was among the wounded. I was wounded in the leg. Since there was no other way out for us, the Chetniks surrounded us and those who were able to walk or were slightly injured were taken to a nearby field. They told us to sit down on the ground and to put our hands behind our heads. Next to me was a cousin of mine who nodded his head towards me and said there were Bato Arnautovic and Dragan Koprivica there. The two approached the dead and the seriously wounded and shot them. I also noticed when they took out their knives, they grabbed Jusuf Suljic, aka Juka, by the head and slit his throat. Also they did the same to Nihad Tomo. One of the soldiers shouted at us, "Bow your heads. Otherwise I'll kill you all." At that moment, from the direction of the houses in Kalkan [phoen], an officer appeared and came close. One of the soldiers, Stevo Petricevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, Witness, please. Witness, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about the description you've just given. In the group of people who were shot at, you said some were dead already. Can you give an estimate as to the number of men who were, in fact, killed in that specific incident who were not already dead?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Around 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were any of those men, of those 15, armed at that moment?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to the arrival of Tintor, which you describe in your statement and you describe it at paragraph 27 of your statement. First of all, could you give me the full name of Joja Tintor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Jovan Tintor. His nickname is Joja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 23, you describe Tintor as the commander of the enemy formation. And elsewhere you referred to him as being in a position of command. What was it that you saw which led you to believe that he was in command?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: First and foremost, a relative of mine who led the group from the village when they went to negotiate at the Butile barracks had Jovan Tintor there, on the other side, as well as Nikola Stanisic and the rest. That's what he told us about when he came back from the negotiations. The second thing I wish to point out is that when we were taken prisoner, when Joja Tintor came to us, he introduced himself to us and he asked whether there were any wounded persons there. And from his military bag he took something out and gave us something to keep us warm. He wore the summer uniform of the JNA. He had a pistol at the waist. He had a military bag, and on his head, he wore a cap with a five-pointed red star.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And what was it your relative had told you, after coming back from negotiations with Tintor, about Tintor's position?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: He said that they had negotiated, that they had demanded that men from the age of 15 to 70 surrender to the barracks and that they would guarantee their safety and security. However, our leaders did not accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Specifically focusing on the question of Tintor's position, what did your relative tell you Tintor's position was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Tintor commanded a paramilitary formation that, in my view, consisted of about 2.000 men. When they arrived - how should I put this? - it was as if they were ants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just one final question: Was there anything else that Tintor said or did that made you believe that he was in command of the paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, while we were sitting there, all these soldiers of his addressed him as Commander Joja. How should I put it? Even before, until Stevo Petricevic came there, he's a neighbour of mine, and he had a radio transmitter on his back, as far as I can remember, it was an RUP 3, a military radio. He addressed him as Commander Joja, what do we do about this, what do we do about that? So he talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to move now to the period that you were detained at the cistern in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up 65 ter 01428, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you're about to be shown a photograph. I'd be grateful if you could tell the Court what the photograph depicts.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: This depicts the compound where the company was, the fuel company. There are two cisterns there, in which we were held prisoner. The smaller one was a petrol cistern and there were about 90 prisoners there, and the bigger one had been used for diesel fuel, and other prisoners were held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask that that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 130.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That can be a public exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be Exhibit P2311.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Which of the two cisterns were you detained in, the smaller one or the bigger one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I was in the smaller one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, how many nights did you spend in that cistern, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: 13 nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe the surface of the cistern? By which I mean the ground, essentially, of the cistern.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: As for this cistern, they made a door there, like two by two metres, and then they put a reinforced door there. There was a chain and a padlock on the door. However, as they cut that opening for the door, there was this 15-centimetre edge that they could not cut through, so that was there by way of support. And that is where water accumulated because it rained, and in -- therefore in the cistern itself, there was always about 15 centimetres of water. In 1985, this has been -- this had been abandoned, this entire terminal --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Let me -- let me interrupt you, Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: -- however, you could still feel the smell of fuel, I mean the odour, bad odour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How were you able to sleep in the cistern if there was 15 centimetres of water on the ground?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: We didn't sleep at all. Whoever managed to tried to lean against the metal wall. Some people would even fall asleep and then fall into that water. That's the way it was, roughly. We were crowded into half of that cistern.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to a person called Hajro Delic. He was detained with you in the cistern; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe briefly what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, as for Hajro Delic, a day after we were brought there, he and his son and their neighbour had been captured. They told us about those details, how they had been captured. However, some two days later, Nikola Stanisic came with Sok and the members of his special unit, and quite simply, they said that they needed to interrogate him about something. They took him away that day and returned him only the next morning. He was all black and blue. He had been beaten that badly. His tongue was swollen as if it were a ball. He could barely say anything. I knew him from before and his son was there as well. We tried to hold him and he just managed to say that Nikola Stanisic had asked him for one million marks in order to release him, and then he and these members of the special unit beat him up. As far as I can remember, they had been involved in conflicts even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did he survive his injuries?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: This is what I wish to say: Just as he said that to me, a woman walked into the cistern, she wore a white coat, and she examined him, and she established at that point in time -- I mean, I noticed that he took a deep sigh and he died. She examined him and gave him some kind of an injection and realised that he was dead, established death.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'm afraid I'm going to have to press on. Could you describe very briefly what happened to Enver Celik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly which date it was, but this Sok, Mile Stojanovic, these four members of the special unit, they had wooden sticks, and there was this short man who came with them, as if he were a child, and allegedly he pointed out Enver Celik and said that he had mistreated his sister. They took him out and took him behind the cistern. However, the cistern nearby was in such a position that those other prisoners could see what had happened. They hanged him on this construction where cisterns were filled with fuel. So they saw him hanging by the arms from that construction, they hit him twice with metal bars, and they broke his backbone in that way, so he never moved afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, this is at paragraph 44, you state that on or around the 10th of June, Zuti came to your container and called ten people out. And you go on to say that you --

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: They had never been heard of or seen again. Do you have any information as to what became of those ten men?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: These men were allegedly taken out for an exchange. As far as I can remember, it was stated that they were taking them to Ilidza. However, as far as I can remember, I never heard of them again. I mean, I heard that they had been killed and some of them were found at Vlakovo, in the city cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to move now to the incident involving the bus. You state in your statement that -- this is at paragraph 50 -- that Serbian police Special Forces arrived armed to the teeth and ordered you to step out in single file and to board the bus. What was it that made you believe that they were Serbian police Special Forces?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: When they came there to the cistern, they stood there in a line of three or four metres. They had black masks on their faces, black and white camouflage uniforms, with those anti-terrorist automatic weapons and ordinary automatic weapons. They had grenades around their waists. I mean, like real guerrillas. Then they ordered us to leave the cistern, one by one, with our hands on our heads. We were supposed to run to the bus. And after we board the bus, we were supposed to lie on the floor, one upon the other, for our own safety, and then we would be taken for an exchange to Kobilja Glava.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to move on. You said that the driver of the bus was Zuti, who had been a driver for Tintor. How do you know that he had been a driver for Tintor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. When he came to the cistern to get those ten other people that he previously took away for an exchange, allegedly, my neighbour Alija Gacanovic was in the cistern too and he used to know him, and he said that he was a member of the Special Forces of Vikic's army, who left after the war started. So I heard that from him. And I saw him then as well, when that van took them and I saw him at the steering wheel on -- in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, very briefly, you said that the bus was accompanied by four cars. Could you describe, very briefly, who you believe were in those four vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: In those vehicles -- well, they were escorting those who had come to get us. I mean they were the ones who brought these vehicles in the first place and the bus too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Who was in the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: These Special Forces members.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: The ones that I could not see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just one intervention, the transcript does not reflect that the witness also said "probably."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you clarify that as well? I wonder whether the witness has answered your previous question, what it was that made him believe that they were Serbian police Special Forces. Did he mean the police from Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'll clarify that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, in your immediately previous question, Witness --

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- you said -- I asked you who were in the vehicles. Did you say that they were Special Forces members or probably Special Forces members?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, judging by the way they were dressed, I considered them to be Special Forces members, a Special Forces unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, my next question is, in the English language, the term "Serbian police Special Forces" is somewhat ambiguous. Could you clarify whether you meant they were from Serbia or whether you meant they were Serbs from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say where they were from, but I know for sure that they were not ordinary soldiers. I mean, it's like in the movies, when you see those anti-terrorist forces. That's what they looked like, with those socks over their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. I'll continue. Witness, I want to take you now to the moment when Zuti got off the bus to put some water into the cooler of the engine. Could you just describe, and keep it fairly short, what you were able to see or hear just when he -- when you -- when he decided to get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: When we came to this place that was called Sokolina, I heard the driver, because on the bus there were two men who were escorts, guards, who asked him why he stopped. He said that the engine was boiling and that he had to add some water into the cooler. What I heard was the stream, the brook, nearby, when the bus stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you describe the nature of the weapons used? In your statement you state that small arms, hand-held rocket launchers and zoljas were being fired. How were you able to tell that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Now I'm going to tell you all about this but I'm not going to take too long. When they got off the bus, for about 10 or 15 seconds -- or, rather, after 10 or 15 seconds, a strong detonation was heard from the front and then gunfire started from small arms, and there were also two stronger detonations. Then hand grenades were going off underneath the bus. This went on for about 15 minutes. Later on, it went quiet. I heard vehicles that were turned on afar, I heard wailing. I was being sensible, and I said, "Try to keep quiet because if they hear that anyone survived, they are going to kill everyone." However, nothing could be heard after that. Vehicles approached the front of the bus. One man got out of a vehicle and said to this person in the other vehicle, and I heard it, he said, "Board the bus and see whether there is anyone who survived." And this other one swore at him, he was using swear words in relation to God and the church and he said that he could board the bus himself and check if he wanted to. And then these vehicles went back to the -- in the direction of Srednja. I mean, I was underneath the dead and I was drinking the blood of my relatives and neighbours. I was on the floor. My face and mouth were on the floor but there was that much blood. It was unbearable. I managed to get out with a neighbour and two more relatives and we managed to get two other men out as well into the nearby forest, about 50 metres away. They died on the spot. So we continued through the forest. Let me try to explain something. Before the war, I was a mountaineer, so I could recognise different places. I could realise whether there would be any settlements nearby. I could also read markings on trees, and luckily, I managed to get to Vukasevici, a Muslim village, where I was received by the then Territorial Defence, headed by Dzafer Heric, who immediately organised two tractors and went to take the massacred persons out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay, Witness --

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: He found some zolja and Osa ammunition and some machine-gun ammunition belts, and then the commander of the Chetnik guard in Srednja arrived with his Chetniks and they tried to hush things up. However, Dzafer said to Dragan Ikanovic, Dragan, there are witnesses who are still alive. He said to Dzafer Heric that he did not see anything, that he is not going into that, that this what is Boro Radic did and Ratko Hadzic. And that's what Dzafer Heric conveyed to me when he came back, all of it, and I saw these weapons that had been used. And that is why I claim what -- that that was used to fire. And all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, in -- could you just specify the precise number of men who were able to get off the bus after the shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Six of us got out. Two of them died immediately after they were out, and the rest were found by the territorials on the next day, when they came to get the massacred persons out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like to show you a video, so if you look at the screen in front of you, we are going to play 65 ter 40159E.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can stop it there. We've stopped at 3 minutes and 14 seconds of that clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you explain what you saw in that video-clip?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I didn't see the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need to broadcast that video otherwise --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we play it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's broadcast only that video-clip. We will play the video again, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll play it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can stop the video now. Thank you. We stopped at 3 minutes and 7 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Court what you saw in that video-clip, please?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: This is the bus that took us there and we were massacred there. As you can see, in the rear part of the bus, you can see a pile of massacred bodies, and even on the outside, you can see blood that was spurting all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your statement, this is paragraph 60, you state that Ibrahim, a photographer from Vogosca, filmed a video. Is this the video to which you were referring?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that as a public exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Finally, I'd like to play another video. This is 65 ter 40159G. And again, if this could be broadcast so the witness can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can stop it there please, stopped at 15 minutes and 2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what you saw in the first part of that clip, please?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: That is the place near Vukasevici village, where the local residents dug a mass grave in which the massacred residents of Ahatovici village were buried. This grave is still there, only The Hague had requested exhumation, and as a result, all these residents had been identified for the second time and are now buried next to the mosque in Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And in the second part of that video we saw human bodies. Could you tell the Court what you know about those?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Those were the bodies of the people who were butchered in the bus. They were pulled out by members of the TO. And with their assistance, since TO was in the area, and was commanded by Dzafer Heric, they were brought up there to this location and buried. They were loaded on two tractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your answer a moment ago, where you said that residents dug a mass grave in which the massacred residents of Ahatovici village were buried, were you referring to the victims of the attack on Ahatovici or to the victims of the bus massacre?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I was referring to the victims of the attack on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember the time frame where the video-clip started? It's around 13 minutes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Finally, Witness, were you personally present for the burial of the victims of the bus massacre?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Alongside my relative, I was there. The other people who were seriously wounded were transported via Olovo and Kladanj to Tuzla. They were supposed to be operated but they only received first aid. My relative and I tried to help with the identification of those massacred bodies. We tried to determine that on the basis of their clothes and things like that because none of them had any IDs on them because all the documents were confiscated from us at the time we were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. That ends the direct examination. There are no associated exhibits to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. We will take a break for 20 minutes, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, you will be asked further questions by Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness. First of all, I would like to clarify a number of issues relating to your village, and then we shall move on to this incident. When did you start preparations for the defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't hear. [Interpretation] I can't hear the witness. You have to switch on that in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, we did not make any preparations for the defence of our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But didn't you state already that you had made some preparations? Did you have trenches around your houses?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Those were not preparations. These trenches were to serve as cover for people from shells. People wanted to survive, and as for women and children, we hid them in the cellars of our houses that we called shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you dig those trenches in your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: It took place on or around the 23rd -- or, rather, between the 20th and the 25th, when the Serbian forces started digging themselves in on the hills around Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did you set up the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: The so-called Crisis Staff, it wasn't actually a Crisis Staff. Those were the village elders or leaders who, at the summons from the Serbs from the barracks, who inherited this barracks after the departure of the JNA, to enter negotiations. However, the Serbian side demanded surrender of all men, which was not accepted. Those were the men who were village leaders, and they were answerable to the local residents of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With all due respect, Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, make sure that you put a pause between his answer and your question. In particular, given the fact that the witness is not with us at this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm kindly asking you that we don't make any generalisations. Let us establish the exact order of move. Is it true that Vahid Alispahic was a high-ranking official of the SDA and he was a high-ranking official in the MUP? Was he the president of your SDA branch?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, I knew that he was the president in town, but I don't know that he did anything in the village of Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you know that Bakir Alispahic, Hasan Efendic, commander of the TO, and Jusuf Pusina, another high-ranking police official, came to Ahatovici often during the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I do know, while I was captured in the camp, Mile Stojanovic, who introduced himself as the prison warden and who said that he was a captain who had been stationed in another army district, and I know that because a relative of mine, Esmar Jusufovic, who is unfortunately deceased, told me later, after the war, that they used to work together. That's how he introduced himself. And whenever he came in front of this cistern where we were locked up, he would mention Bakir Alispahic, who allegedly promised exchange at Kobilja Glava and the women and children at the Bozica pump, he actually said that Bakir Alispahic had no people for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us be precise. Is it true that this Crisis Staff was formed in 1991, "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the head of this Crisis Staff, as its commander and the commander of the TO, was Hasan Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your amalgamated statement, in paragraph 5, did you say that Mujkic, Hasan Mujkic -- give me just a moment, that in March of 1992, during negotiations between representatives of the SDA and SDS, it was decided by the Serbs to ask the Muslims to vacate the village of Ahatovici and that this was conveyed to you by Hasan Mujkic, representative of the village, who attended the meeting? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, but he was a representative of the residents of Ahatovici, a representative, and nothing else. He wasn't a commander and he wasn't a military person. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 41 Serbs, voters, are asking 1500 Muslims to move out of the village, is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I know that they made that request, that they said that we should surrender at the barracks and that our safety would be guaranteed, and that pertained to men between 15 and 70 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did the war start in Sarajevo, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, the war -- the media war and every other war, as far as I'm concerned, started when my village was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that the war in Sarajevo started on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How was it possible, then, for the Serbs to ask you, in March, to surrender, and 41 of them asked 1500 of you to surrender in March, before the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know if it was March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can Mr. Ram show you your statement because that's what it says in your statement under item 5, to the effect that in March, negotiations were held and that the Serbs were requesting you to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: That's not correct. I know that there were negotiations in May, when Hasan Mujkic went there, and then he returned and told us what the other side wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say, that the Serbs had erected barricades and that they checked people at those barricades and their identity cards were inspected. When were these barricades erected?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, sometime between 20 and 25th, while they were preparing an attack on Sokolje village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which month?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But up until then, you could move freely without any checks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, the barricades around Ahatovici were set up earlier, I don't remember the exact date, on the bridge near Butile barracks, where at present there is cattle market. There is a bridge on the River Bosna and that's where one barricade was, so in order to pass through there, you had to be inspected. It was possible to go to -- through the forest to Visoko via Bioca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was this barricade erected and how long it stayed there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: This barricade was still there when I was taken prisoner and taken away to Butile. And after that, when we were transported in a military bus from Butile to Rajlovac, all these barricades were there. They had to remove those iron beams in order to allow the vehicles to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was nearly two months into the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Not two months. The war that I recollect, and everything else, started on the 25th of May when Sokolje came under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But up to that point, you didn't have any problems with the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any problems because I was trying to survive. I was working in Blazuj and sometime in February or March 1992, my foreman told me not to come to work anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's dwell on the barricades. You say that people were stopped there and that their IDs were checked, and that the people manning the barricades had certain lists. Does that mean that they were looking for specific people and that if the people were not on the list, they were let through?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. While the bus was travelling between Dobrosevici and Stup, it was mostly women who travelled. Men didn't dare venture out, and they would tell us what they saw on the way, after they would return, and what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 65 ter 90224, this is another statement of yours, you said that the Serbs were checking the people while they were going to work.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. We heard that from the women upon their return from town, because that is what they saw. If there were any men on the bus, they were probably Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, there were your women, Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. And they witnessed when people were checked, their identification papers were checked. And that's what they did at the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of your statement, didn't you say that while you would go to work, you would come across these barricades, and the Serbs checked identity of the passengers by looking at a list and they compared the names with the names on the list? Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. When I was travelling to Blazuj, already in Blazuj, near the company where I worked, they were erecting barricades and checking people's IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read your paragraph 7. Unfortunately, I have to do it in English. That's your amalgamated statement, page 3: [In English] "Since I travelled to Sarajevo daily by bus, at that time, due to the presence of the -- these Serbs, check-points and barricades, I feared to come to work. The Chetniks who manned these check-points used to stop the buses and search them with the pretext of searching for weapons. I noticed that during these searches the Chetniks checked the Muslims rather than the Serbs, who travelled in them. They always asked for our identity cards and checked them with a list of Muslim names which they had. I do not know on what basis this list was prepared. However, no one was arrested in my presence. I have not seen this list but I am aware that it was prepared in March 1992 and consistent -- consisted of Muslim names whom the Serbs thought were trouble-makers." [Interpretation] Is this what you stated?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: All of this was happening in Blazuj, at the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it says here that you travelled from Ahatovici to Sarajevo, in which case you don't pass through Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, but at the time there was no barricade on the bridge in Bojnik. When I reached Stup and then Ilidza, and from Ilidza by bus to Blazuj, at the Mostar intersection in Blazuj there were already barricades erected and IDs were checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Witness, Blazuj is not in Sarajevo. Ahatovici is closer to Sarajevo than Blazuj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. And I said where they performed these checks in Blazuj. If I said barricades, I didn't say that there was a barricade in Bojnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to this. It says here that you were afraid to go to work any longer. You don't say that you were sacked from your job by your foreman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have much time, Witness, let us clarify something. You can freely say what you wish. Any answer will do, as far as I'm concerned. Is it true that in Dobrosevici you bought and obtained weapons before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. Well, some people did but I don't know about that. People who had money and whatever, perhaps they did buy some. I know that in Ahatovici, there was a registered hunting society, and then from Dobrosevici, Kobilja, Bioce, this was a hunting society and these people had hunting guns. Some people even had two. Before the war people had pistols as well. And I'd like to point out that in Ahatovici, and in part of Dobrosevici and the surrounding area, there were some active duty policemen as well of the reserve police force. They had had automatic weapons issued to them. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at 65 ter 22187?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is your statement from the 15th of April, 1993. Could it please not be broadcast because of the name. The second paragraph contains information that you gave, that you had, about 150 small arms and that these were actually semi-automatic and automatic rifles. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I meant semi-automatic and automatic weapons that active duty policemen had as well as the reserve police force. There were only about 15 pieces or so. All the rest were hunting guns. They -- the hunters also had carbines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 17 of this document? And I'm going to read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 17 of the document says -- so here it is. It's the second line from the top: "To that end, we bought weapons individually, exclusively infantry weapons, that is to say, pistols, guns, all the way up to semi-automatic and automatic rifles. With a view to better organisation and defending the village, we established a Crisis Staff and it was headed by Hasan Mujkic, son of Jakub. We had about 150 weapons. In addition to Hasan Mujkic, on the Crisis Staff there was Mujkic Husein, Mujkic Sefko, Gacanovic Cazim, Gacanovic Muhamed, Novalija Meho, Mujkic Fikret, Mujkic Dzemal ..." Is that true what you stated in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, look. Again you're saying Crisis Staff. These are village leaders, the village elders. You can call them the Crisis Staff or whatever. I told you no one could forbid the people to buy weapons and whatever. However, even if there were who knows how many weapons in the village, if you look at guns, tanks, Pragas, on the other side, and then there is this village in Lijeva [phoen] that is surrounded by barracks, and also around Ahatovici, even if some people did buy weapons out of fear, so what? To defend their own homes, their own door step, no problem with that. As for Ahatovici, I know about 50 men were there, able bodied --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Let me understand the situation, how the witness is able to see the document. Is he seeing the document through e-court or has he the document in front of him? Probably Court Deputy in Sarajevo can help us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have the document here, but we're not sure of the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever a specific document is referred to, please help him to read the document. We are on page 17 of his statement. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 22187, Mr. Ram, and it's page 17 in this longer document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, while it's being found, I don't call that the Crisis Staff. You were calling it the Crisis Staff. And you say who headed it. In the next paragraph, you say that the Serb population moved out, in mid-May, from Ahatovici to Butile and Reljevo. Are you trying to say that, in mid-May, the Serbs, the Serb population, went to the barracks in Butile to stay there, to live there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: They left their homes and they went down there to Bojnik, where Serb areas were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Butile, does that mean that they went to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I consider that to be Serb territory at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Butile barracks of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this same statement you say that you stood guard around the village, and then, on the 25th of May, you received an ultimatum from the former JNA and the local paramilitaries to surrender your weapons, and this was done through a loud speaker.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. An armoured vehicle was moving about and they used a loud speaker from the school in Dobrosevici, and they were asking for surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were calling for a surrender of weapons, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, surrender. Well, generally speaking. I mean of men, too. And probably they meant weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take your statement where it says that you should hand over weapons. It doesn't say that you were supposed to surrender?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: This is what was said very nicely, that men should surrender, whoever has weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this paragraph on the first page of your statement? "On the 25th of May, 1992," do you see that paragraph? Page 17 of this compound document, on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It would be more convenient if you read out the ERN number so that the Court Deputy can be -- can identify the proper page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here that you should surrender your weapons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out: "On the 20th of May, 1992, we received an ultimatum from the former JNA and local paramilitaries to surrender our weapons. This request was issued by guards around our village."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This request came over a loud speaker. That's what it says, right? You skipped one line.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: "This request came over a loud speaker. Of course, we did not agree to this, and we continued to stand guard around our village." That's right. But they were issuing this ultimatum to us for us to surrender as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So why didn't you say that in this statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, I cannot think of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then, on the 27th of May, you say you were attacked. By what kind of forces, how many soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, that is after the attack at Sokolje, on the 27th, because they did not manage to take Sokolje, they just turned their weapons, because Ahatovici is to the left. All the hills around Ahatovici, Serbs were there, they dug in there with their heavy weapons, and the barrels were just turned in this direction. Let me just tell you one more thing. You can see the barracks of Butile and Rajlovac from my house, and the entire farm, and also the area where the tanks were placed. On the hills you saw Pragas that were dug in. It's about 100 metres away from my home as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Can I please ask you that we do not speak in so general terms. Let us focus on these details. Were you attacked by infantry from Dobrosevici or by artillery on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: On the 27th, shelling started and, from time to time, there was gunfire coming from side arms, probably to scare the population, and to show force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say that you successfully repelled that attack without any losses on your side. How could you repel an artillery attack? Were you attacked by the infantry from Dobrosevici and you managed to repel the attack? Look at this very same page, the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I have to explain this a bit. I was in the lower part of the village because up above Ahatovici you could hear infantry gunfire, things like that. It's possible that someone was attacking. Perhaps the guards were trying to repel the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say, in another paragraph, on the 20th of June, 1997 -- 65 ter 22187, we had called it up a few moments ago. Let's just see which page we need. You say that attacks on Ahatovici took place on the 27th of May from Rjecica and Rajlovac at 2300 hours, but the villagers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The villagers responded with gunfire and repelled the attack. For defence we only had about 50 small calibre weapons. So how many did you have as stated?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: The entire village had between 50 and 150 weapons, as far as I could tell, roughly. And I did say that it came from the area of Do. It's on the other side. There is this small river there, this brook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say here that you were attacked from the direction of Rjecica, the brook, and from the direction of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. That was behind the part where we were, this brook, and Rjecica was behind us, where our guards stood, and that's above Ahatovici. That place is called Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you suffer any losses on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were people wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement given on the 15th of April, 1993, you say that you repelled the attack and sustained no losses; whereas in your statement of the 20th of June, 1997, you say that two Muslims were killed and about ten wounded. So which is true?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: What is true is that they were wounded, that people were wounded. As for two Muslims, I heard in the village that they had committed suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why would they commit suicide?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Most likely -- four women committed suicide with them, probably out of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why is that not mentioned anywhere in your statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, it just depends on what I remembered at what point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-hah, all right. Let me now read parts of the statement of Mujkic Edin, which is 65 ter 22184. You don't have that part with you. I will read it out to you. He gave that statement and on page 2, and over on page 3, he says: "I learned later on that commander of the Territorial Defence of Ahatovici, Mujkic Hasan, decided to flee before his men. He's a former policeman, and he fled together with his brother and deputy Husein and his uncle, Junuz. They reached Visoko via Krstac hill." And then on page 3 it says: "I emphasise that the enemy found, in his house, lists of fighters with weapons issued to them. It was typed on four pages. I saw these lists in the hands of aggressor officers. They used these lists in order to determine the status of each one of our captured soldiers. In relation to that, they particularly tortured those fighters who had been issued with a sniper or with a mortar." So you had the names of fighters, taking the whole of four pages, together with information about the weapons issued to them. Among them there were people who had snipers issued to them and mortars, sabotage mortars. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you build two shelters, two fortified shelters in your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No, no shelters were built. Those were simply houses who had very strongly built basements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were they reinforced? What did they use to reinforce them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No, this was just a basement area, cellar area, that was made out of concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Did you have trenches or not? And then back in 1991, did you have them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Not in 1991, but in 1992, in May, depending on where people lived and where they had houses, people would dig out an area in order to hide there, near their houses. And I apologise but let me tell you that I had no weapons whatsoever, nor did I have any need to attack anyone or kill anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mention here that the barracks were just across. Was it the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: There were two barracks. One was called Orao, which was a factory, and the other one was the Butile barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in mid-1991, there was a mobilisation of reservists of the Yugoslav People's Army due to war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I know about that. But let me tell you, I also was a reservist in the barracks called Koran, at Pale. They called me up sometime in 1988. If you remember, there were exercises, manoeuvres, held of the Yugoslav People's Army. I think that the whole operation was called Nevesinje 88. Please correct me if I'm wrong. It was quite sometime ago. And then in 1990, they called me to come to Lukavica. There was an entire battalion there, mostly Muslims and Croats, who were dismissed. They returned their equipment and they were sent home without being given any other assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say 1988?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. But actually during that period of time, I'm not quite sure, it was a long time ago. Perhaps you know better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters. In Ahatovici, did you manufacture weapons, ammunition and explosives?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there could have been something of that nature without you knowing about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask you, since we do not have much time, and we would rather not recall you to come back to complete your testimony, let us just focus on the most important things. You say that the main attack on Ahatovici commenced on the 29th of May, that they used Howitzers, 105- and 155-millimetres multiple rocket launchers, mortars, tanks and similar weaponry. How did you come to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. It was an all-out attack from all directions, from both barracks, from the surrounding hills, such as Tijekovac [phoen] Koprivica, Paljevo. From the entire area that had been taken by Serbs around Ahatovici, they started shelling, and it lasted some three days, as far as I can remember. Everything was on fire. My house was knocked down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I regret about your house, but let us look at this, Witness. You mentioned 4.000 shells. How did you come to conclusion that 4.000 shells had fallen?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I gave it as a rough figure. There were numerous shells, innumerable shells that fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many Serb fighters, Serb soldiers, attacked you on the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the exact number but there were thousands of them. They came from all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one place you said 1.000, in another place you said 2.000. So there could have been more than 2.000?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, listen, that's my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you undertake any offensive operations prior to that against surrounding Serb villages and the Butile barracks? Did you undertake any offensive operations against surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. I personally didn't. But some people that had weapons, most likely they did return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was the leader of the Green Berets and Patriotic League in your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Patriotic League and the Green Berets had been established back in early 1991?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I know that they were established, but I don't know that any of them were present in Ahatovici. I know that we received some misinformation that there were about 500 members of Green Berets in Ahatovici, which is simply beyond comprehension, as though it rained members of the Green Berets in Ahatovici. We didn't have that many residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Weren't there 1500 Muslim residents in Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. But many residents fled as a result of fear. They fled to their relatives in the city and surrounding towns, Visoko, Breza and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it was mostly women, children and the elderly who went to stay with relatives?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Also younger people left, because the parents took them with them. They didn't allow them to remain back in the village. When the attack started, people were fleeing all over, in panic. Some managed to flee via the forest. Some came across minefields. All kinds of things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we see 1D3261? I hope that you have that in hard copy in front of you. 1D3261. Could we see it in e-court, please? Unfortunately we don't have it yet but I will read it out to you. This document comes from the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, and this is the bulletin of daily events number 114. It says here that there were places where sniper fire was opened in Dobrinja and Vrace. And then in the second paragraph it says: "Green Berets and other Muslim paramilitary formations which, yesterday, on the 29th of May, 1992, attacked parts of local commune Dobrosevici, villages Bjelugovici, Mihaljevici and Bojnik, were repelled and pushed into the -- into the school in Dobrosevici and from the village of Bioce in Ilijas municipality, and then surrounded in the village of Ahatovici. The Serb army issued an ultimatum to these paramilitary groups in the village of Ahatovici to surrender by 30th of May, 1992, by 1800 hours." So you attacked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Yes, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I simply want to inform the Court that an English translation of this "SRNA" press release -- sorry, of this document, excuse me, is available at 65 ter 00298.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see it in the e-court and we can put aside the Serb version because I've read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph, before the heading "Banja Luka CSB." Witness, so the Green Berets attacked the Serb parts of the local commune of Dobrosevici. They were repelled, pushed back to Dobrosevici and then given an ultimatum to surrender. It was only then that an ultimatum was issued to have soldiers surrender, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what is stated here is not true. Just like when I was in the camp in Rajlovac, when I was imprisoned in the cistern, they came with a prewritten text and those people who had no visible injuries were given these texts to read out while the cameraman from "SRNA" was filming it, and these people had to lie in front of cameras.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, please, let us not waste time because we will need ten hours instead of two.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: So this is not true. Did you capture a single member of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will get back to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D3262, which is where police report the events on the next day. I hope this document has been translated too. This is the bulletin of daily events number 115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here, constant sniper fire in the area of Grbavica, Vrace and Dobrinje is what Muslim groups used to provoke and so on. And then the next paragraph, in the Serbian village of Rajlovac, local commune Dobrosevici, village of Ahatovici, the Green Berets carried out an attack on the Serb houses in the villages of Bojnik, Bjelugovici and Mihaljevici. The attack was repelled during the night on the 1st of June, 1992. Muslim terrorists were encircled. In the village of Ahatovici they are putting up resistance, but the village is under the control of the Serb army.
