Witness, let me ask you: In your statement given on the 15th of January, 1998, you said that they captured all of your civilians. So were you a civilian on that day or were you a combatant?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Which date did you mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 1st of June, 1992, you were pushed back into Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: This is when the village Ahatovici was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in relation to that, you say that women and children were separated and then transported to the industrial centre. And they arrested all of us civilians. So were you a civilian?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a hard copy of the English translation of this document. I can provide the hard copy to Your Honours right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I take it Mr. Karadzic has done with that document, right? Do you need to continue with that document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I am done with this, only this part pertains to Ahatovici. We don't need to deal with this document anymore. We can use it for some other locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time. It's time to take a break. This time we'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please take into consideration the possibility that we might need more time? It is well known that people from Bosnia, we, who come from Bosnia, like to talk at length. I would prefer him to focus on the answers, but at any rate, I would appreciate if additional time were granted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at half past 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what kind of military specialty did you have in the army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Technical service. I underwent three months of training and after that I was appointed a courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is someone who is a courier good with maps?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yeah, well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now discuss groups that you mentioned. Do you call all Serbs Chetniks or were you referring to some specific groups based on their insignia and their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I was referring to specific groups according to their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you are not calling all the Serbs Chetniks and extremists?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us now which specific groups you observed and identified, what kind of uniforms they had, and what kind of insignia they wore?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: They had fur hats with a cockade, with four Ss. They had bandoliers and bayonets and weapons. Only a few of them had rifles. The majority had automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement when you are making reference to Serbian Special Forces, did you mean those groups?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. When I said Serbian Special Forces, I was referring to the soldiers dressed in camouflage uniforms who had Red Berets on their heads, that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that the Serbian Special Forces wore masks.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. Those who came to the camp where we were, allegedly to take us for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you noticed White Eagles and Arkan's men. How did you distinguish between the two?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: When I was taken prisoner in Bojnik, Zoran Damjanovic told me about Arkan's men. In fact he says, "You will be taken over now by Arkan's men." As for the White Eagles, they had white ribbons on their sleeves and around their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, this man Zuti that you mention was a member of Vikic's unit of Special Police, is that the same Vikic who remained as the commander of the Muslim Special Police, the notorious Vikic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, that's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this person Zuti was a member of Special Forces. Are you sure that such member of Special Forces would be a simple driver for Mr. Tintor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I heard that from Alija Gacanovic, a neighbour of mine who knew him, and he said this is Zuti, he's a member of the former special unit of Vikic, and the driver of Joja Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of the 30th of October -- just a moment. No, no, thank you. I'm sorry. You say that a woman wanted to kill some people because her brother had been killed by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you make any mention of a student who wanted to take revenge on his teacher while he was a young man?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the fighting in Ahatovici, did you have any combatants outside Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. We didn't. Those were not combatants. Sometime in May, from the direction of Visoko, four men were brought down there who originated from Bratunac, who were actually captured in Bratunac and were imprisoned in the school, and they were exchanged in Visoko. In order for them to be exchanged they were brought to Ahatovici and they were supposed to proceed to Sarajevo. However, it was impossible for them to travel any further and they remained in Ahatovici. I remember that the two of them had the last name of Salkic, and another two were brought with these two. They were all active-duty soldiers of the former JNA who had fled Vukovar and were brought there. They didn't have any weapons with them. I remember the name of one of them, Ramiz Peljto.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Witness, if I tell you that we captured some men several times, do you realise then that these men from Bratunac had come there to fight again once they had been exchanged?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. They just wanted to pass through and head for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I'm sorry, they had relatives in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say here, on page 4 of your statement, that Nikola Stanisic used to have some personal problems with the man called Sok, and that that was a good opportunity for him to settle the accounts with him.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it wasn't Nikola Stanisic who had problems with Sok. Sok was the commander of the unit that mistreated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. I'm sorry. Delic Hajro, you say, told us that at the initiative of Nikola Stanisic, with whom he had some problems before, was beaten by Sok as if it was Nikola Stanisic who had ordered that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm trying to keep up with the various statements that the accused has referred to, so if he could just -- every time he refers to a statement could he tell us which statement he's referring to, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, that's the witness [as interpreted] of the 15th of April, 1993, given by this witness, and on page 3, at the bottom, and on page 4, it says that Hajro Delic told how -- about how he had been beaten up and then he said that that was done at the initiative of Nikola Stanisic with whom he had some conflicts before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then on the same page, page 4, towards the bottom, you said that a woman called Mladjenka asked the guards, a couple of prisoners, so that she can execute them because allegedly we, the Muslims, had killed her brother Mladjen in Ahatovici, and that the guards removed her and drove her away?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, there is reference to the guards when Zuti threw tear gas or some other gas to the cistern, and as soon as he went away, the guards opened the cistern up and saved you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5, you say that on the 14th of June, at around 1830, Ramiz Peljto was taken out by his former colleagues, two of his former colleagues, from the JNA, that he had abandoned, and that you had never seen or heard of him again. Was there something between those three?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, look, as far as I know, the two who came there were dressed in camouflage uniforms and they called the name of Ramiz Peljto, claiming that they allegedly went to school together. They took him behind and I never saw him return. Immediately after that, members of the Special Forces came, packed us on to the buses and drove us away where they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know or is your village in Novi Grad municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Joja Tintor was associated with Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I know that very well. Joja Tintor and my late father were friends. My father was born in Ahatovici and my grandfather, my late grandfather, being elderly people, they knew each other. There were brotherly connections among these people and I really don't know who could have driven a wedge between them, and how a human being can do something like that to another human being. Now, Joja Tintor had friends in Ahatovici that he used to visit. Anyway, I would see him in passing, and to this day I believe that he was a nice man. I saw him when I was taken prisoner, and he sent us in a file -- and these soldiers were taking us. But as soon as he came, all these things that were happening stopped. He gave us bandages to dress our wounds. I never saw Joja Tintor again, but I know that he owned a restaurant in Vogosca. I know where his family house is. They used to attend burials, funerals, at the Serbian Orthodox cemetery. For example, the funeral of Dusko from Rajlovac, we all attended the funeral. People knew each other. They were perhaps not nodding acquaintances that didn't need to socialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But during the attack you did not see Joja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw him after the attack. Who told you that he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: That's how the soldiers addressed him, Commander Joja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Maybe if I add something it will help. On the ex-JNA uniform that he wore he had three stars on each epaulette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he had a five-pointed star on his cap?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I must tell you that the last person on this earth to put the five-pointed star on his cap would be Joja Tintor. Could that have been perhaps someone else?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. When we were imprisoned in the camp, this man Sok, whose full name I don't know, used to wear a flag on his shirt, the Yugoslav flag, and also another flag on the right-hand side of his cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I told you that he never liked either Yugoslavia or the four-pointed star -- now, you were taken out of this detention and put on the buses on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many men were in the bus?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say that you were all lying on the floor of the bus?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: In the rear of the city transport bus, if you can imagine how big this space is, which is only the space for standing, we were lying face down, one on top of the other, like sardines in a tin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In how many rows, all 50 of you or whatever number you said?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Two rows. And in between, between those rows of seats, there was some more space.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you in the first row and was someone lying on you or were you in the second row and was someone on the other side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I was in the first row. I was the third one to get out of the cistern, and I lay there by the back door of the bus, right next to the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many men were lying over you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: All of them. There were like five men lying on me. It was crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Five rows or five men or in two rows? How many rows were above you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: One row, but there were five, one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And inside, in addition to yourself, how many did you say were there, 50, 55?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: 55, 55. Packed, no one was allowed to sit down where the chairs were. At the entrance, this guard, who had this black mask on his face, he was hitting people in the back and he was saying, "Going to -- go into the back of the bus, lie down, face down."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there were two guards there in addition to the 55 of you packed like sardines?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Two guards and a driver, of course, this Zuti, who I know as Zuti, and who came with a van in front, and Alija Gacanovic said that he was a member of the Special Forces of Dragan Vikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you went from Semizovac to Srednjevo [phoen], right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: We set out towards the gate, to the right, to Rajlovac, across the railroad. You know very well that you go right to town and to the left you go to the Vogosca intersection, and from there, you go to the right to Kobilja Glava and to the left to Semizovac. And then from Semizovac to the right and on the right is Ilijas. Let me just remind that you had family members in Gora, which is a village near Srednje, if you know the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Gora, the predominant population is Croat, right? So you took the right-hand road towards Srednjevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, to the right from Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you pass Srednje or did you turn before Srednje?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: When you pass the bridge, in Srednje, we passed underneath somehow, and we turned, and that is where the barricade was, and I heard the driver ask, Where is this, what place is this? And this man said Srednje. And he also asked how much more to this place called Sokolina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that along that road towards Gora and Bozic, that's where the separation line was, right, or the front line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you turned right and you came to this place called Sokolina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, look, in Srednje, we turned left, and that is where this conversation took place, and then we went straight ahead. Then I felt that we were on a macadam road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But if you had turned left, you would have gone to Bozici. Straight ahead you went through Vukasevici and Visevice; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Sokolina along the road between the villages of Visevice and Vukasevici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Also, there is a sawmill there that was processing wood, logs, from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your hearing is pretty good, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You heard a vehicle escorting you behind the bus, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. No. When we set out from Rajlovac, I saw two vehicles straight ahead, and two vehicles behind us. These two vehicles were following us. I heard them all the way up to the barricade in Srednje. When we took this macadam road, I no longer heard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Vukasevici is a Muslim village in Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know that they are in Serb territory, but I know that it is a Muslim village. Next to Vukasevici is the Serb village of Drazevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Vukasevici, at that point in time, had a Territorial Defence which helped you, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then at one moment, you said that you heard a big explosion, right, and after that you also heard automatic gunfire, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, a strong detonation, explosion. As I was lying in the back part, I felt this detonation behind my back. There were masses of people. Everybody was shaken. Glass was shattered. We heard wailing. Well, look, that cannot happen if a bullet is fired. It can only be a 100-millimetre rocket launcher or zoljas. The Territorial Defence, when they took out the massacred men and brought them to the spot and showed them there, and down there, there were members of the Serb army as well, headed by Dragan Ikanovic, until then they were negotiating. You know where Gajevi is, at Cevljansko Polje, where the hunting lodge is, of the former president, the late president Tito. That is where they met and where they negotiated all the way up until the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the Visevice is a Serb village, and this Dragan -- is Dragan actually from Visevice or Srednje?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: From Visevice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Vukasevici is a Muslim village and they had reached an agreement, and I can refer to folk poetry to describe this, but it meant that no one would touch anyone.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: That's right. It was just this road where the massacre was committed that was separation line, as it were, from Visevice. And then from Visevice, a road had been made -- or actually, it was made later on, from this hill, where these locals took me. And they showed me trucks and trucks, going from Vogosca, and they were driving something, but I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was this shown to you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: During those days between the 16th of June and, well, further on, because I stayed there with my uncle for about 11 days, for rehabilitation and recovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Vukasevici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How was it that you got wounded? Did you enter the bus as a wounded man?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. My big toe on my left foot, it was grazed by a bullet and also my upper leg was grazed by a bullet. This was before the massacre. However, during the massacre, my upper left arm was hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And wounded as you were, you got up and left with your colleagues. Were any of them wounded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My neighbour, a young man who was about 15 at the time, his arm and his leg were wounded, and my uncle was wounded -- I beg your pardon, his private parts. And my relative was wounded with a large calibre bullet, it must have been a 7.9, in the arm, up here, sort of somehow it went length wise through his arm. And then his leg. And then I, with the help of my uncle, who was a pretty strong man, so we managed to help each other and also we helped those two. We were so afraid but I realised that they were alive, sort of, Rizvanovic Safet and the other colleague, and we just got them out through the window. Oh, it was unbearable. And it was in the nearby forest, we got them out there. It was about 50 metres away. And then they died there in the forest because they had been so badly injured. Let me just mention, Mr. Karadzic, that I had been a mountaineer, a boy scout, that I did my military service in the army, that I know, because there was a transmission line there, that I would reach some village, and on a plateau I could hear fire. So I didn't want to go that side. I went to the other side where it was peaceful. The road brought me, luckily for me, to these Muslim villages. And let me say one more thing. Up until then, negotiations were taking place. And let me say one more thing. When the massacred men were being buried, a Serb from the village of Drazevici came and said that his wife died when she heard of this case, when these Muslims who had not attacked went out there and helped him to bury his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us try to explain this. The two men you got out died soon afterwards, and you also said today that three men who remained in the forest died and were later found massacred. Does that mean --

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No, no. No, no. Those three hadn't died. What I said was that three more men were found after the Territorial Defence arrived but they were pretending to be dead. They didn't know who it was until they saw TO on the shoulders of these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Muslim TO was wearing its own insignia in Serb-held territory, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know about that being Serb territory at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On whose territory was the bus hit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Where the separation was, right in the middle of the road. That's where the bus was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the separation line, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And wounded as you were, how long did it take you to get to Vukasevici, how long is the road between Sokolina and Vukasevici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But, look, an area that is unknown, fear, everything else, when we got out of the bus -- and let me point out one more thing. The rain that started to fall, it was all over the ground. We just remained in our T-shirts and underwear, and throughout the night we walked through the forest, and I managed to find some dirt path as well, and I could crawl there, and I was trying to check whether land mines had been planted there. And it's only towards daybreak that I reached that village. Somehow I first tried to realise who was living there, whether there were any sheep or pigs, or what kind of clothes people were wearing. So this young man who was 15 years old, we told him to go towards the house and to shout, "Neighbour, help." We said to him that if everything is all right, he should get in touch with us, let us know that everything was all right. If he doesn't get in touch afterwards, then we should go on running.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please try to keep the answers as short as possible so that we don't take up too much time? So we did see that on the 16th -- or, rather, on the 15th, in the morning, this Ibrahim recorded this with a camera. Why didn't he get closer? Why did he stay so far away? Was it because of the separation line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No. Look, he was up there because when Dzafer Heric, the then commander of the Territorial Defence up there, there were about 30 or 35 territorials, arrived. However, when they were getting the massacred people out and towards the end, Dragan Ikanovic came with his own fighters and with two trucks in order to trail the bus away. Probably to cover up. I don't know. I can only guess. However, three days later, they came and they set the bus on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now try to keep it simple, Witness. Serbs -- two plus two Serbs, two guards and two drivers, are driving 55 prisoners on a bus. Then they use an explosive device to hit their own bus and the explosion is strong. Then they fire at their own bus in order to ruin it and in order to hit some Muslim inside if they are lucky, and then they leave everything the way it was, and then the Muslim Territorial Defence arrives. They get the dead and wounded outside. They record it with a camera. Can you explain this to me? How is it that the Serbs found that to be useful for their own purposes, to do that and to leave the bus right there on the spot?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, look --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He started, yes, just a second. Yes, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My objection is this. It's quite all right for the accused to put a summary of the incident to the witness but the summary is inaccurate. He says: "Serbs -- two plus two Serbs, two guards and two drivers." I mean the evidence is quite clear. There was a bus and four vehicles escorting the bus. There were two guards on the bus plus the driver. That's point number 1. Point number 2, I don't think there has been any evidence so far that the Muslim Territorial Defence took the wounded off the bus. So if Mr. Karadzic is going to summarise the incident, I submit that he should do so accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. He's absolutely right, Mr. Karadzic. Be cautious citing evidence when summarising evidence and putting it to the witness. Probably, Mr. Witness, having had the benefit of hearing Mr. Gaynor, now you should be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say in your statements that on the following day, on the 15th, the TO came from the Muslim village of Vukasevici to pull out the dead and wounded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true, and did you state this and was it true when you stated it, that in the morning, on the 15th of June, the Territorial Defence from the Muslim village of Vukasevici reached the bus in order to pull out the dead and the wounded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, they came with two tractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it was then that they filmed the bus, from the hill, from an elevation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't the hill. It was a road, a path, used by horses to transport logs, and there was a stable there where the horses were kept, the horses used to pull out logs from the forest. And let me tell you something else. When I managed to get out, when I managed to go up, the territorials left immediately, and the TO men had their own scouts, and their scouts followed the situation as it unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So we have resolved that. The Muslim TO came to pick up these people. Did the Army of Republika Srpska join them or perhaps another regular military formation headed by this Dragan, did they come on the same day, did they analyse what had happened?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Witness, I will put this to you, this hypothesis. This bus was hit by some sort of an explosive. It was either a mortar or a rocket launcher, and then they started firing on it, and it was a sort of an ambush and people in that ambush killed those on the bus and just left them there. Do you know exactly which unit attacked you and who did this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I can't say. I didn't see who fired at us. I didn't see anything. All I know is that once they had brought in the massacred people, Dzafer Heric said that Ikanovic had said that he knew nothing about the case and that it was the doing of Boro Radic and Ratko Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show everyone here 65 ter 30836, please. With all the reservations we have concerning the intercepts, let us see what is it that Momcilo Krajisnik and his brother discussed on the 15th. I regret that you don't have the document there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The witness is -- the Sarajevo office does not have this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We do not have the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have it, all right. Can you see what's on e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I read it out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before putting the question, if you could tell the witness the nature of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have in my hands here, in hard copy, and we also have it on our screens, the intercept of a conversation which took place on the 15th of June, 1992, and it is a conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and his brother Mirko Krajisnik. Krajisnik Momcilo is at Pale in the assembly, whereas Mirko Krajisnik is in Rajlovac in his village of Zabrdje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will skip the first two pages in the Serbian -- rather, three pages in the Serbian version, and then we will go straight to page 0736, which is page 6 in this document in Serbian. Could we find the corresponding page in English, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And for you, sir, I will be reading this out in the drama style, theatre drama style. Mirko says: "What is it?" Momcilo says: "Well, running around all day." Mirko cursing devil and saying, "I heard that the Muslims who were running away from Misoca killed a full bus of Serbs in Srednje, Misoca was being cleansed." Momcilo: "Yeah?" Mirko: "So Muslims killed a full bus of Serbs," and then Mirko says, "who were on their way to Pale as refugees. Just a little while ago, they told me that this wasn't the case but that, in fact, they took these prisoners with them. Actually an old sergeant who does exchanges up there received a phone call from the city, can you hear me?" And so on. And then the following page in Serbian, Krajisnik says: "So they called them from the city. Alispahic, what was his name, and he said those prisoners had been killed. Momcilo: "What prisoners?" Mirko: "They took the prisoners to Pale again." Momcilo: "Uh-huh." Mirko: "And then at Srednje, they were intercepted by Muslims who killed all those prisoners. Our two men were heavily wounded." Momcilo: "They thought those were our people." Mirko: "They thought those were our people too. Momcilo: "Yeah." Mirko: "And tonight they want to retaliate against all Serbs in the city and in prison." Momcilo -- or rather, Mirko says: "And allegedly, they will use their cut-throats to attack Rajlovac in groups and all kinds of things like that." Do you see, Witness, that this first explosion is a completely illogical attack on the bus, as a result of which two Serbs were wounded too?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know how long they fired for, how long they fired on the bus. I know what they used to fire. What do you think, that two, three lengths of ammunition belts for machine-guns were enough, the so-called Gorenje. They fired over 1.000 bullets, and we saw casings that had been brought from up there. How did they end up being there? They didn't just fall from the sky. Then we saw all those casings of zoljas and other ammunition used from rocket launchers. I saw them as they fired at the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not challenging that. I'm asking you only: Was it only the Serbs who had rocket launchers, bombs and zoljas, or did Muslims have them too?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't care who had what. What I know is that genocide was perpetrated, a massacre, a completely incomprehensible killing of people, helpless people. And let me just tell you that the day before, on the 13th, when women, children and men were exchanged at a petrol station, in Boric -- in Bozic they then put us into refrigerated trucks and they drove us along the same road. They only opened the door when we reached Sokolac. Some people suffocated on the trucks. They urinated there. They fainted there. They drove us up there to Rogatica, and to Koran, where I used to serve as a reserve soldier of the former JNA, and then they took us back to Pale, to the old boy scout centre in front of the Panorama Hotel, and I know it from my time as a boy scout. And then they let us get off the refrigerator trucks. I met then somebody called Sasa, who used to serve in the army with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be nice to hear all that if we had time but let us go back to our topic. What you described was much before the event with the bus. Now that you have mentioned the exchanged -- the exchange which took place at the Bozic petrol station, let me tell you what happened. The Bozic petrol station is between Rajlovac and the city, and this is where women, children and the elderly from Ahatovici were exchanged -- rather, they were allowed to enter the city of Sarajevo. Was that the exchange?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, that was the exchange. However, those of us who had been kept in the smaller cistern were boarded on the refrigerator trucks, and Mile Stojanovic told us that we were going to be exchanged at Kobilja Glava. However, they took us all the way to Rogatica, and then again, in the evening hours, they took us back to fuel cisterns. There were no longer any women, children, or the elderly there. In my view, they did it in order to hide us, to conceal us from UNPROFOR so that UNPROFOR wouldn't find us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So was that an exchange? Did any Serb civilians leave Sarajevo on that occasion? Or perhaps it wasn't an exchange, was it simply the case that the women, children and the elderly from Ahatovici were allowed to enter Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: It was an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who left Sarajevo as part of that exchange?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: From Sarajevo, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did some civilians come from the Muslim part to the Serbian part of Sarajevo, or was it only the case that the Muslim women, children and the elderly were allowed to enter Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we've concluded with that. That was on the 15th. We don't know whether it was an exchange or simply women, children and the elderly from Ahatovici were allowed to enter Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, as for the able-bodied residents or, rather, prisoners, they were transported on the following day to the place where this happened?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes. When we returned in the evening, let me tell you, the Serb guards who were there, even they were surprised to see us back. They were surprised that we had been brought back. We spent that night, nobody slept during the night. In the morning they brought some awful food, just salted water. I ate bread that was all covered in mildew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I understand you, I understand you but we have to go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 30839, 65 ter, please? Another intercept intercepted by the Muslim state security. Could we see it in e-court, please? I will tell you what this is about. This is a conversation where Camil calls Mirko Krajisnik and then they have a conversation. So: "Hello, Mirko, Camil here," and so on. Could we see the next two pages in Serbian, please? Camil says: "Well, let me tell you," he curses a relative, and he says, Well, let's see if we can find something equivalent." And then Camil says: "Edin Brajlovic seems to be here in the Rajlovac barracks." And then Mirko says: "Edin Brajlovic." And then Camil says: "Yes, from Ahatovici."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know this Edin Brajlovic from Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Zuti took Edin Brajlovic in the van and he was never seen again. I also know Zijo Brajlovic. It was a family there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: There is a witness who is their relative and who says that Edin Brajlovic was killed, and that he was found in some grave and then later buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we see that Camil is searching for Edin Brajlovic, and then Camil says: "Is he there at Rajlovac?" And then the other man says: "No, there is nobody here." And then Camil says: "So there is nobody there, so that means that we had a wrong piece of information." And then Mirko says: "No, for sure, believe me." And just to tell you this conversation took place on the 20th of June. And then Camil says: "Somebody told me, somebody called me." And then Mirko says: "No, everything -- everybody who was here was exchanged. You know, 284." Camil says: "Yes." And then Mirko says: "I think that about 50 of them were released beyond all requests or outside of all requests," and so on. "The Gacanovics and the Martinovics and the rest were sent to Pale, part of the people, as you know, got killed," and then they continue talking. And he says: "Parts of the people went up to the central for exchange," and he says, "as a matter of fact, they are going somewhere to Sokolac?" So on the 20th of June, they mentioned this exchange, 284 were exchanged, 50 were released to go home, then Gacanovics and Martinovics are mentioned, and then Mirko says: "You heard some of them got killed." Obviously he's referring to the bus. Sir, Witness, can we agree that first there was a detonation which made all the glass on the bus shatter, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you still believe that the Serbs would destroy their own bus if they wanted to kill somebody? Wasn't it easier to take that person out and execute?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Listen, that was not a Serbian bus. That was a city transport bus that had been confiscated by them. It was not an army vehicle. It was a state ownership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes, but that was a city transport bus that had been confiscated. We were loaded onto this bus with the intention of killing us, as was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, a little patience, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted into evidence, the first and the second ones, but, of course, with all the reservations that we have, and could it be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think it's fair to press Mr. Karadzic right now as to whether he accepts these an authentic intercepts or not. And if he does not accept that they are authentic intercepts, on what basis is he tendering them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Having issued the decision on intercepts, I think it's about time to hear the parties' argument and deal with it. But before we do that, can you answer the point raised by Mr. Gaynor, Mr. Karadzic, as to the authenticity of these documents you are tendering? Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just answer the point with respect to intercepts. Our position is that with respect to intercepts, we put the Prosecution to its proof to prove the reliability of any and all of the intercepts. However, because the Chamber has decided to allow them to do that at the end of their case or later on in their case, we don't want to be disadvantaged by not using those intercepts that would be useful to our case, in the event that the Chamber finds that the intercept procedures were reliable and they are admitted. So that's the basis on which we are proceeding. So our position is that it's up to the Prosecution to establish the reliability of intercepts in general, and if they do that, then our intercepts should be admitted as well as theirs. And we still have -- reserve the issue of the pre-war intercepts, which you've already ruled on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not that you are having it both ways, you are tendering them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we are having it both ways, exactly, because we are taking the position that the Prosecution has the burden of proving that the intercepts are reliable and so we don't want to waive that issue. But in the event that you find them reliable, then he we also will want -- we wouldn't want to be deprived of having the ability to use intercepts to our advantage, so we are having it both ways in that sense, but I don't see anything wrong with that. It's not our job to prove that these intercepts are reliable or unreliable. That's the burden of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will not spend too much time on this today. So what if we find those tendered by the Prosecution reliable and then you did nothing about the intercept you tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, when we hear the testimony of the Bosnian officials who intercepted these conversations, I think that that testimony will apply to our intercepts as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will mark these two intercepts for identification following our practice.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits D1088 and D1089, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It's time to have a break. We will break for 15 minutes this time. We will resume at 10 to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, for your re-examination, five minutes would be sufficient, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It would indeed. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could conclude by 25 past. If you could conclude by 2.25. You have about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I do intend to conclude much earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not going to go into any other details and minutiae. On page 11, you said today that a man called Enver Celik had maltreated somebody's sister and that these men took him out, hanged him and beat him up for that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you never mentioned the fact that he had been hanged? How come?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I did mention that. I don't know how this was not recorded. I'm sorry, I have a document here with me compiled after the massacre, when I was doing the identification of the bodies, and it is written here, Hajro Delic and Enver Celik were murdered at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, was it really possible for someone to do something bad in the past and then someone comes to take him out, beat him up and eventually kill him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Listen, I can't tell you that. I know that Enver Celik and the late Esad Celik, his brother, and they had a third brother as well, whose name I don't know, they were - how shall I put it? - they liked to enter into brawls and fights. They had tattoos. So he recognised this man as the one who abused his sister according to the tattoo that he had, and these followers of his took him out because of that. And you know how -- this structure for loading such big cistern that has the capacity of 8.000 tonnes, so they hanged him on that structure and they beat him and they broke his spine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if we take all this into consideration, if it hadn't been for the guards, these incidents would have happened more often; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Look, I'm not going to mention the name, but there was a guard whom I knew very well. We used to meet each other in a restaurant and treat each other with drinks, so when he was on duty in the evening, he would bring me bread and the packet of cigarettes. And he would tell me, Just go back there into the dark, so that no one would see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to thank you, Mr. Witness, and allow me to express my regrets that you are on such bad terms with your neighbours and that everything happened as it did.

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the first point relates to the village of Misoca, which was referred to in one of the intercepts that you saw. Could you clarify the ethnic makeup of the village of Misoca before the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Before the war, there were only Muslims living in Ahatovici, only those roads separated Dobrosevici from Ahatovici and Bioce. So this was a kind of dividing line between these villages. The Muslims lived in Ahatovici, Dobrosevici were predominantly Serb-populated, although there were some Muslims and Croats as well. Bojnik was predominantly Serb. Bioce was a Muslim village, Rjecica, Rajlovac also --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The question was about the village of Misoca. What was that village before the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Misoca was a mixed village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Misoca at the start of --

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: I think the Muslims were a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And did they remain a majority throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the moments after the shooting stopped in the bus incident. And I want to focus, first of all, on the question of the escort cars. In your statement, you said, at paragraph 52, that no cars could be heard anymore behind the bus. And in your statement at paragraph 53, you said that after the shooting had finished, you heard the cars in your escort start and that the criminals went away from the scene of the crime. Could you clarify whether the escort cars, according to what you were able to hear, accompanied the bus to the location where shooting took place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: When we reached Srednje and when bus set off towards Sokolina, I no longer could hear those vehicles. However, when we arrived in Sokolina, when the massacre was committed, I felt -- once the shooting stopped there was the smell of gunpowder, of blood, but I felt that some vehicles were being started. People were crying because they were wounded. And I told them to be quiet because if those outside heard them, they would come into the bus and kill us all. These vehicles came parallel to the bus and you know what happened later, that the one from the first vehicle said, Go in and check, the other one responded in foul language and didn't go, and all of them went back to Srednje from where the bus had come. Now, let me make this clear, in Srednje, when I was not able to hear those vehicles, I believe that they had gone to set up an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you and the other survivors managed to get off the bus, were the vehicles still at the location?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want you to focus now very much on the time when the driver said he had to get off the bus to put water in the cooler part of the engine. Do you remember that specific moment?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, how much time elapsed between that moment and the start of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: KDZ041
utterances.text: Ten, 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Enough for them to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Tribunal and this Chamber I would like to thank you for your giving it notwithstanding all the difficult situations you are in. Thank you. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this will be it for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As you wish. We are prepared to start with the next witness, as you wish, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we do that? Then we have 25 minutes. Let's proceed. Let's bring in the next witness. In the meantime, I just received the witness list for next week. Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question was whether it is subject to change that may occur during the course of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's fair to say that it is subject to change. If tomorrow's witness, we are talking about Dr. Zecevic, I presume, if he indicates that he wishes to testify, we are prepared to amend the appearance in order to permit that, facilitate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Did I hear tomorrow? I think we are on leave tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the initial appearance for Dr. Zecevic is scheduled to take place tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you, it doesn't concern me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: My name is Ramiz Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, did you previously testify in the trial of Momcilo Krajisnik and have you previously provided information to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in 2004 I testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you, with the assistance of an interpreter, review an amalgamated statement which contains relevant portions of your previous testimony and other information you've provided?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I ask for 65 ter 90219, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see on the screen in front of you an electronic copy of the first page of your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we move to page 6 of this statement? I'd like to direct everyone's attention to paragraph 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, I understand that paragraph 27, I'll summarise it briefly for you, it states that you've been shown a page of a document which states that: "Tesanovic sought the approval of the president, on 30th of May, 1992, in order to commence shelling at 1800 hours. This is consistent with and must be a reference to the shelling of Ahatovici on 30th May 1992." That ends the reading of that paragraph. Is it correct that you wish to remove that paragraph from your statement?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I asked for that because it's not truthful. The shelling started on the 29th, so I don't see any reason for him to ask for the shelling to commence on the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Subject to the deletion of that paragraph from your statement, do you adopt that statement as your evidence, and if questioned today about the same subjects, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: After having made the declaration that I would speak the truth and nothing but the truth, I would like this to be removed because this is not the truth. The truth is that the shelling started on the 29th and lasted the whole day on the 30th. So there was no agreement and there was no ultimatum possible at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Subject to that correction, Mr. Mujkic, do you adopt this amalgamated statement as your evidence in this trial?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little intervention. The witness said that the shelling lasted for 24 hours and it's not been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic did you say that the shelling of Ahatovici lasted for 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And that's true because the tanks fired during the night, the upper part of Ahatovici close to the forest, and then from 4.00 a.m. until 10.00 p.m., mortars were firing at houses. So there were several of them and each of them had their own area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. We will come to that in a moment. I just want to complete one formality, that you do adopt this statement as your evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2314, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll now read a summary for the public of the statement which has been admitted. Mr. Mujkic was a resident of Ahatovici prior to the conflict. Its population was primarily Muslim. A Serb check-point was established near the village and Muslims were not allowed to pass. Its establishment is reflected in an order issued by the Rajlovac municipality Crisis Staff. Several of the Muslims in the village were lightly armed. On 9th of May, 1992, the Muslim village of Sokolje was intensively shelled. Ahatovici was also shelled from 29th of May to 2nd of June, 1992. Communication lines were cut. The shelling was followed by a Serb infantry attack. Mr. Mujkic, who was armed, left Ahatovici on the 31st of May, 1992. He encountered Serb soldiers coming from the Muslim village of Gornja Bioce, which was deserted. On 3rd of June, 1992, Mr. Mujkic returned to Ahatovici. It was also deserted. The Muslim houses in the village had been burnt and the mosque had been destroyed. An excavator was digging holes and soldiers were throwing bodies into a hole. Four years later, in 1996, bodies were exhumed from three locations in Ahatovici. One location contained the remains of four women, including Mr. Mujkic's sister and her daughter. Mr. Mujkic later learned that the surviving Muslim population of Ahatovici had been transported to and detained in three locations next to Rajlovac barracks. The military-aged men were detained in two fuel cisterns. Mr. Mujkic hid in the forest for two months until his capture by Serb soldiers on 6th of August, 1992. He was transported in a military truck and detained in Rajlovac barracks, where he was interrogated and beaten. One of his interrogators placed a grenade in his mouth and hit his chin, breaking his jaw. On 9th of August, 1992, Mr. Mujkic was transported to a hospital and was later transferred by Serb military police to Planjo's house, a detention facility in Vogosca municipality. Mr. Mujkic comments on several records of the Serb Municipality of Vogosca. One records Mr. Mujkic's arrival at Planjo's house. Another is a record of the rental of Planjo's house for its use as a prison. The third is a list of 143 men detained at Planjo's house. Mr. Mujkic says detainees at Planjo's house were Muslim and one was Croat. They were routinely subjected to grossly humiliating treatment. One male Muslim detainee was ordered to eat cigarette ends and then to perform oral sex on another male detainee in the view of the other detainees. In another instance, a detainee was asked if he could swim and was then ordered to strip naked and to dive head first from a balcony of the building onto the ground beneath. Mr. Mujkic's brother-in-law and his nephew were among the Muslim men from Ahatovici detained in a cistern next to Rajlovac barracks. Both men were killed on around 14th June 1992, when a group of Muslim men were taken from the cistern, placed on a bus which was driven to a location where the bus was fired upon. 13 members of the Mujkic family were killed in the incident. Mr. Mujkic states that prior to the conflict, the area around his village was inhabited by over 1.000 Muslims. A document issued by the Serb red cross in October 1993 states that by that time, there were no Muslims in Rajlovac municipality. That ends the summary. I will begin the examination-in-chief. I'm not sure I'll finish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic, what municipality was Ahatovici in?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Novi Grad, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up now, please, 65 ter 01660. This is a decree on the promulgation of the Law on the Establishment of Rajlovac Municipality with headquarters in Rajlovac. This record is taken from the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska and reflects a decision signed on the 15th of May, 1992. And the decision was signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We see, Mr. Mujkic, under Article 1 of this law -- would you just -- you see that it says that Rajlovac municipality consists of the territory of Novi Grad municipality? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in Article 2, we see a number of settlements are named. Could you just look at the names of the settlements in that article?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Can it be zoomed in a bit? The Sarajevo Rajlovac municipality encompasses the following areas: Bojnik, Dobrosevici, Ahatovici, Crkotina, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkic --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I know all of that geographically speaking. I live there. I know all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the -- your town of Ahatovici was primarily what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the census in 1991, there were 1.130 Muslims, 920 Serbs, in the territory of the local commune of Dobrosevici. I state that clearly. And that included Ahatovici, Dobrosevici, Mihajlevici, and Bojnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, looking at the areas named in Article 2, outside your local commune of Dobrosevici, were there other settlements named in that Article which contained Muslim populations?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: In Zeljevo there were about ten Muslim houses. In Rjecica none whatsoever because that was a Serb settlement. Then Perivoje is also Serb populated. Although that is the municipality of Vogosca, not Novi Grad. That is also where the oldest Serb cemetery is in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see any other settlements where Muslims lived in this list of names?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Here, no. Well, there is Bacici up there but that never belonged to Serb territory, or, rather, it wasn't taken. And this part, Brijesce Brda and Bacici, Halilovici also, that never fell into Serb hands and there are quite a few Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My question is: Prior to the conflict, in the areas that you've just named, there were significant Muslim populations there, is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that for admission, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2315, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to the mosque. Did you attend the mosque in Ahatovici prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that the mosque was "our symbol and our fulcrum." Those are the words you used. Could you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, the mosque had all the legal documents that were needed in the former Yugoslavia, and it was built in the 1960s. So it was a centre. Actually it was a symbol of the Islamic faith, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What role did the mosque play during religious holidays, for example?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Well, during Ramadan, religious rites were performed there, prayers were held. It wasn't used on every day, except for Friday and the month of Ramadan and then the holiday of Ramadan. So there weren't prayers every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to skip on now, due to time, I'm going to have to move to another part of your evidence and I want to move to your arrest, when you were arrested and taken to Rajlovac barracks. Was that after your leg had been injured?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was wounded on the 6th of August in my right leg. I was taken there on a stretcher, put on a truck and brought to Rajlovac barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Upon arrival at Rajlovac barracks, did you receive medical treatment for your leg?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, no one got close to my wound. As a matter of fact, they broke my teeth there and my jaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to the very early morning of the 7th of August, 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I survived all of that and I'm going to remember it for as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So in the early morning of the 7th of August, 1992, your leg was broken and your jaw was broken. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You were visited in the very early morning of that day while you were in detention; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. A Major Vladislav Apostolski arrived, he was commander of the Rajlovac brigade and the military police, and three men followed behind him. He said to me, "We want to ask you something." I recognised this man, it was Nikola Poplasen, because I saw him at different meetings, as I followed political developments. He was among the top leadership of the SDS party so we saw him on TV all the time. The other man was Mirko Krajisnik, who I knew personally. And the third man wore a uniform and he had a well-groomed beard. I would recognise him now, but he did not introduce himself. He didn't say a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How long had you known Mirko Krajisnik at this stage?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I knew Mirko Krajisnik for quite a while, but the last time we sat next to one another was at the funeral of one of his relatives towards the end of April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you describe the nature of the interrogation that took place?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Nikola Poplasen put a question to me, where is Hasan Mujkic, where is Husein Mujkic and where is Elvir Mujkic. Hasan Mujkic was a policeman before the war and he was commander of the TO of Ahatovici, the Territorial Defence of Ahatovici. His brother Husein was also on the Crisis Staff. And my son, who was 20 years old, had fled from the JNA. They knew about that. And they probably would have skinned him alive in front of me. They were looking for the three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You weren't able to speak during the interrogation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: I was covered with blood. My broken jaw was covered with blood. And I said that I couldn't speak. Then Poplasen said, "Oh, he's a literate one, I can see that. Give him a pen and paper. Have him write all of this up and send it to me." After they had left and that was it, and then Apostolski brought me a pen and paper and said, "Write. You heard what the vojvoda said."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mirko Krajisnik was present with Poplasen during that period, was he?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ MUJKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But he didn't say anything either. Probably according to this hierarchy, excuse me, this Chetnik hierarchy, Nikola Poplasen was the top man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I can stop there if you want, Mr. President. I see we are just about at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we'll -- we have to adjourn for today or for this week. And next week we start on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. And we remain available, should Dr. Zecevic decide to testify, we are available to deal with that as Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we probably would not be available to hear his testimony on Monday, given the need for our expert to come and consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me see. We are supposed to sit on Monday -- no, we are not supposed to sit on Monday. There is no sitting on Monday. Unless other things take place, we will resume our hearing your evidence on Tuesday, 2.15. Have a nice weekend. Mr. Tieger, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one possible matter to enhance flexibility, if there is any possibility of the Defence remaining in contact with their expert, and ensuring to the maximum extent possible that should events transpire, so that we know somewhat in advance of what is now an unexpected hearing date, that her absence won't delay that and she attempts remain available to the maximum extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll do our best, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is now adjourned.
